claim: The overview recommends keeping CLAUDE.md under 200 lines and moving growing reference material to skills or splitting it into .claude/rules files.
why: Files loaded at session start contribute their full content to every request.
check: Use 200 lines as a review threshold for each loaded CLAUDE.md and look for occasional reference material that could load on demand.
quote: Keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines. If it's growing, move reference content to skills or split into

claim: Use a blocking hook for a tool action that must always be prevented, since a rule in CLAUDE.md or a skill is an instruction Claude can miss.
why: A PreToolUse hook that blocks the edit enforces the rule at tool execution.
check: For critical tool actions forbidden in CLAUDE.md or a skill, check whether a hook or deny rule actually blocks them.
quote: An instruction like "never edit `.env`" in CLAUDE.md or a skill is a request, not a guarantee.

claim: Hooks fire on their lifecycle events without Claude choosing to invoke them, while Claude interprets skill instructions and the outcome may vary.
why: Use hooks for actions that must happen the same way every time and skills for workflows that need Claude to interpret instructions.
check: Check whether a fixed action that must run on a matching event depends on Claude choosing to run a skill.
quote: Fires on its event without Claude deciding

claim: Hooks cost context only when their output is added to the conversation, while skill descriptions load by default at session start and full skill content loads on use.
why: Loading strategy differs per extension point and drives context cost.
check: Check whether frequently triggered hooks add verbose messages to the conversation.
quote: | **Context cost** | Zero unless the hook returns output | Description loads each session; full content loads when used |

claim: CLAUDE.md gives Claude standing project instructions, and the active output style gives it standing instructions about role, tone, or response format.
why: Claude follows both as instructions, so enforcement of an action that must happen every time needs a hook.
check: Check whether response preferences users may want to switch off are kept in a selectable output style and project facts that apply across styles are in CLAUDE.md.
quote: Both give Claude standing instructions. CLAUDE.md carries what Claude should know, and an output style sets how Claude responds.

claim: MCP gives Claude tools and data access to external services, and skills can supply guidance or workflows for using those services.
why: They solve different problems: connectivity versus know-how.
check: When Claude needs access to an external service or repeats a workflow with it, check whether the setup supplies the needed connection and any task-specific guidance.
quote: MCP connects Claude to external services. Skills extend what Claude knows, including how to use those services effectively.

claim: In the main conversation, using a skill adds content to the main context, while a subagent uses a separate window with its own input and output tokens and returns a summary.
why: Choose a subagent for context isolation, parallel or specialized work; choose a skill for reusable reference or invocable workflows.
check: For a task that reads many files, check whether Claude could do the work in a subagent and return only the summary to the main conversation.
quote: Uses a separate window with its own input and output tokens

claim: Claude decides what subagents run next turn by turn, while a dynamic workflow uses a script to sequence jobs that need many workers or cross-checked findings.
why: The docs distinguish who controls sequencing: Claude per turn versus a script.
check: For a job that outgrows a handful of subagents or needs findings cross-checked, check whether a dynamic workflow would handle the sequence.
quote: With subagents, Claude decides turn by turn what runs next. In a workflow, the script decides:

claim: A plugin is the packaging layer that bundles skills, hooks, subagents, and MCP servers into one installable unit, for reuse across repositories or distribution via a marketplace.
why: Packaging lets teams reuse the same setup across repositories or distribute it through a marketplace.
check: Check whether a setup maintained in multiple repositories could be shared through a plugin.
quote: A plugin bundles skills, hooks, subagents, and MCP servers into a single installable unit.

claim: Plugin skills are namespaced like /my-plugin:review so several plugins can coexist without name collisions.
why: The plugin namespace keeps identically named skills from different plugins distinct.
check: If plugins share a bare skill name, verify the invocation uses the intended plugin namespace.
quote: Plugin skills are namespaced (like `/my-plugin:review`) so multiple plugins can coexist.

claim: Same-named skills resolve managed > user > project, subagents resolve managed > CLI flag > project > user > plugin, and MCP servers resolve local > project > user, while CLAUDE.md is additive and matching hooks merge.
why: A duplicate name can shadow the intended skill, subagent, or MCP server, while overlapping hooks can fire for the same event.
check: Check for same-named skills, subagents, and MCP servers that shadow the intended definition, and for overlapping hooks that both match an event.
quote: when the same name exists at multiple levels, one definition wins based on priority (managed > user > project for skills; managed > CLI flag > project > user > plugin for subagents)

claim: When CLAUDE.md files at different levels conflict, Claude uses judgment to reconcile them rather than applying a deterministic precedence.
why: CLAUDE.md files from different levels contribute to the same context.
check: Check user, project, and subdirectory CLAUDE.md for contradictory instructions.
quote: When instructions conflict, Claude uses judgment to reconcile them.

claim: All registered hooks fire for a matching event regardless of whether they come from user, project, plugin, or managed sources.
why: Hook registrations merge across sources.
check: Run /hooks and look for overlapping registrations that both perform the same action on a matching event.
quote: all registered hooks fire for their matching events regardless of source

claim: Startup CLAUDE.md files, active output-style instructions, and model-invocable skill descriptions cost context on each request, and connected MCP servers load tool names and server instructions up front.
why: Too much extension context can fill the window and make Claude miss relevant skills or conventions.
check: When reviewing context cost, account for full skill content and MCP schemas on use, subagents in separate windows, and hooks only when their output is added to context.
quote: Every feature you add consumes some of Claude's context.

claim: With disable-model-invocation: true, a skill stays out of context until the user invokes it, which the overview recommends for skills with side effects.
why: It saves context and prevents Claude from starting the skill on its own.
check: Check whether a skill with side effects can run automatically when it should require user invocation.
quote: Use `disable-model-invocation: true` for skills with side effects. This saves context and ensures they run only when you name them.

claim: Claude matches tasks against skill descriptions, so vague or overlapping descriptions may cause it to load the wrong skill or miss a useful one.
why: A clear description helps Claude judge when a model-invocable skill is relevant.
check: Review skill descriptions for vagueness or overlap between skills.
quote: If descriptions are vague or overlap, Claude may load the wrong skill or miss one that would help.

claim: A fresh custom subagent starts with its own system prompt, while the built-in Explore and Plan agents start without CLAUDE.md or git status.
why: A fork loads the parent conversation, system prompt, and tools.
check: Check what the subagent receives at startup, and restate critical instructions in the delegation prompt when using Explore or Plan.
quote: The agent's own system prompt, not the Claude Code system prompt

claim: The built-in Explore and Plan agents skip CLAUDE.md at startup.
why: The guide recommends restating the instruction in the delegating prompt when Explore or Plan needs it.
check: If a setup relies on CLAUDE.md to steer search or planning subagents, verify the instruction is passed in the delegating prompt.
quote: The built-in Explore and Plan agents skip `CLAUDE.md` at startup.

claim: Claude Code recommends adding extensions as recurring needs appear, such as putting a repeated mistake or review comment in CLAUDE.md.
why: A repeated task prompt or playbook suggests a skill, repeatedly copying inaccessible data suggests MCP, and an action needed every time suggests a hook.
check: Check which recurring need each extension addresses, including whether a second repository needs the same setup and could share it as a plugin.
quote: A repeated mistake or a recurring review comment is a CLAUDE.md edit, not a one-off correction in chat.

claim: Output styles are the intended place for response voice, length, format, or a non-engineering role, switchable one at a time.
why: You can switch the active style when you want a different kind of response.
check: When you want to toggle response length, tone, format, or role, check whether those preferences are configured as an output style.
quote: A voice, length, or format you want in every response, or Claude working as something other than a software engineer

claim: Path-scoped rules (.claude/rules with a paths: filter) load only when Claude works on matching files, so language- or directory-specific guidance should live there instead of in CLAUDE.md.
why: This keeps CLAUDE.md focused and saves context.
check: Flag CLAUDE.md sections about one subsystem or language that could be a rule with paths:.
quote: with a `paths:` filter so it only loads when Claude is actually working there

claim: Per-directory CLAUDE.md fits when directory owners maintain conventions versioned with the code; a central path-scoped rule fits when you want all conventions in one place or one rule spans scattered paths.
why: A per-directory CLAUDE.md lives with its code and loads at launch from that directory or on demand, while a central path-scoped rule loads when a file matches its glob.
check: Check whether directory owners maintain their conventions with the code or need a central rule that covers several paths.
quote: You want all conventions in one place, or the same rule applies to many scattered paths

claim: Only write down in CLAUDE.md what Claude cannot find by reading the repo or would otherwise spend time rediscovering every session.
why: Current models read the repo very well, and each CLAUDE.md line takes attention on every task.
check: Check for file layout, framework choices, or conventions that Claude can readily infer from the repository.
quote: Only write down what Claude can't find by reading the repo, or what it would otherwise spend time rediscovering every session.

claim: A useful CLAUDE.md records what Claude cannot readily infer, including exact verification commands, how to run a single test file, and guidance you have had to repeat twice.
why: Each loaded line takes attention on every task, so reserve space for useful details such as misleading parts of the code and decisions the repository does not record.
check: Where the repository has test, typecheck, or lint commands, check whether CLAUDE.md gives Claude the exact commands it needs.
quote: How to confirm work in this repo: the exact test, typecheck, and lint commands, and how to run a single test file

claim: The current docs list 'describe your architecture and file layout in CLAUDE.md' as advice to stop following.
why: Architecture and layout already apparent in the repository consume context if repeated in CLAUDE.md.
check: Check whether architecture summaries and directory trees in CLAUDE.md merely repeat information Claude can readily infer from the repository.
quote: Claude reads the repo itself. Only write down what isn't in there.

claim: If Claude keeps missing an instruction, keep its wording plain, shorten a file where it gets lost, and use a hook or deny rule when the rule cannot bend.
why: Current models follow plainly worded instructions, and extra emphasis mostly makes Claude over-apply the rule.
check: When Claude repeatedly misses an instruction, check whether added emphasis is substituting for a shorter file or enforcement of a rule with no exceptions.
quote: piling on emphasis mostly makes Claude over-apply the rule

claim: Keep the enforced set of hooks and deny rules small, and leave preferences with exceptions in CLAUDE.md.
why: Each hook or deny rule needs maintenance and can fire when it should not.
check: If there are around forty hooks and deny rules, review which are preferences Claude could weigh on its own.
quote: If you ever find yourself at forty of them, most are probably preferences that Claude could have weighed on its own.

claim: Use command, http, or mcp_tool hooks for deterministic enforcement and set onFailure to "block" if a crash or timeout must stop the action.
why: Prompt and agent hooks rely on model judgment, and onFailure set to "block" prevents unchecked execution when a deterministic hook fails.
check: For command, http, and mcp_tool hooks that must block on a crash or timeout, verify that onFailure is set to "block".
quote: A `prompt` or `agent` hook asks *another model* to decide, so it isn't deterministic either. For real enforcement, use a `command`, `http`, or `mcp_tool` hook, and add [`onFailure: "block"`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#block-the-action-when-a-hook-fails) if the action should also be stopped when the hook itself crashes or times out.

claim: Deny permission rules hold in every permission mode including auto and bypassPermissions, which makes them the right place for never-read rules like .env.
why: Deny rules continue to constrain actions even in modes that otherwise reduce or bypass permission prompts.
check: Check that files Claude must never read have a matching Read deny rule rather than relying on an instruction in CLAUDE.md.
quote: `deny` rules hold in every permission mode, including auto and `bypassPermissions`

claim: A WebFetch domain deny rule does not stop curl to that domain unless the sandbox is on, and a Read deny rule does not catch a script that opens the file.
why: Rules match tool calls, not intent.
check: On macOS, Linux, or WSL2, check for sandboxing alongside permission rules when the shell needs filesystem or network limits.
quote: A `WebFetch` deny rule for a domain does nothing about `curl` to that same domain, unless the sandbox is on.

claim: Bash deny rules match the literal command string, not the underlying executable, so Bash(rm *) does not block /bin/rm or find -delete; use a PreToolUse hook or the sandbox for a hard guarantee.
why: Command-text matching can be sidestepped by an equivalent form.
check: For a command restriction that must hold across equivalent invocations, check whether a PreToolUse hook or the sandbox covers what the Bash pattern misses.
quote: Bash rules match the literal command string, not the underlying executable

claim: Auto mode uses a classifier to judge actions, so rules that must always hold belong in deny rules or hooks.
why: The classifier can be wrong, and a restriction stated only in the conversation can be lost when it compacts.
check: Check that safety-critical prohibitions are not left to auto mode or conversation text.
quote: Auto mode is a classifier model judging each action rather than a hard rule.

claim: Keep "$defaults" in each configured autoMode list to extend its built-in rules, and put personal autoMode configuration in ~/.claude/settings.json because the classifier ignores project settings.
why: Without $defaults, a configured list can replace built-in context, exceptions, or blocks such as those on force pushes and production deploys in soft_deny.
check: Inspect autoMode in settings for a missing $defaults or a project-level autoMode block.
quote: The `autoMode` block also has to live in `~/.claude/settings.json` rather than the project, because the classifier ignores `autoMode` in project settings.

claim: By default, Claude Code lets Stop or SubagentStop hooks block the end of a turn 8 times in a row before overriding the hook.
why: CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP can raise the limit when more iterations are needed, and 0 disables it.
check: Check whether a Stop or SubagentStop hook that needs more iterations than the cap has a suitable override.
quote: (default: 8). Set to `0` to disable the cap.

claim: Give Claude a runnable pass/fail check, and when the repository already has one, record the command in CLAUDE.md as the most useful line in the file.
why: Claude stops when work looks done, and without a check the user becomes the test suite.
check: Check whether Claude has a runnable verification step for the task and whether an existing repository check has its command recorded in CLAUDE.md.
quote: Claude stops when the work looks done.

claim: Ask for the verification command and its output or a screenshot, whether the check uses a prompt, /goal, a Stop hook, or a fresh-subagent /code-review.
why: A separate model checks /goal after each turn, a Stop hook enforces completion up to its block limit, and /code-review gets a fresh reviewer.
check: For a long background run, check which completion mechanism fits and whether Claude was asked to show the evidence it produced.
quote: "All tests pass" on its own tells you very little, and reading the output is faster than rerunning the check yourself.

claim: When asking a subagent to review against a spec, tell it to skip style and report only correctness gaps.
why: A reviewer asked to find problems will always find something, and fixing every finding adds abstraction and tests for impossible cases.
check: Review prompts and reviewer agents for an unbounded 'find issues' instruction.
quote: If you fix every finding, you end up with extra abstraction layers and tests for cases that can't happen.

claim: Restricting a custom subagent to tools: Read, Grep, Glob makes a read-only reviewer whose limit is enforced by Claude Code rather than requested in a prompt.
why: Tool allowlists are deterministic; prompt restrictions are not.
check: For a custom reviewer intended to be read-only, check whether its tool list is restricted to Read, Grep, and Glob.
quote: that limit is enforced by Claude Code rather than requested in a prompt.

claim: Subagents send their own requests against the same usage and can take longer when they need to gather context the main conversation already has.
why: The default model is the same or smaller, so delegation itself offers parallelism or a fresh reviewer instead of a stronger model.
check: Check whether parallelism, independent review, or another documented benefit justifies the cost of delegating the task.
quote: What they cost you is mostly tokens, since every subagent sends its own requests and they count against the same usage as your main conversation.

claim: Use model: haiku in the definition of subagents doing simple jobs (collecting importers, checking links), and ask for short summaries back.
why: Haiku costs much less per request and simple jobs do not need the larger model.
check: For a subagent that does a simple job such as finding importers or checking links, check whether Haiku fits and whether the prompt requests a short summary.
quote: Haiku is a good fit for subagents doing simple jobs.

claim: Within the docs, the best-practices page says 'use subagents to protect your context window' is outdated advice, while the features overview still says to use a subagent when the context window is getting full.
why: The two official pages weigh the context-isolation benefit differently; best practices says running out of context is now rare and each subagent costs extra tokens.
check: Check whether subagents serve parallel work, noisy-output isolation, or independent review, and account for the extra requests when judging token cost.
quote: Running out of context is rarely the problem anymore.

claim: The best-practices guide discourages routine instructions to keep going or loop until done because current models usually carry on through an agreed task.
why: Most current models have a 1M-token window with automatic compaction, and effort controls thinking depth while phrases like “think hard” are ordinary prompt text.
check: Review blanket persistence reminders and aggressive context management, and keep task-specific completion checks where they help.
quote: lines like that are more likely to cause over-work than fix a stall

claim: Phrases like “think hard” are ordinary prompt text within the current effort setting, and ultrathink asks for deeper reasoning for one turn.
why: Effort controls how long Claude thinks, and ultrathink leaves that setting in place.
check: If a prompt uses “think hard” as if it raises effort, check whether an effort change or one-turn ultrathink matches the intended scope.
quote: Those phrases are ordinary prompt text that nudges Claude within its effort setting rather than keywords that raise it.

claim: Fable 5.2, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 default to medium effort.
why: Higher effort gives Claude more time to check edge cases and verify work, which costs more time and tokens.
check: Check whether effort matches the work: high or xhigh for easy-to-miss cases, low for quick iteration, and max for hard problems Claude should work through unattended.
quote: Claude Fable 5.2, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 default to `medium`, which is plenty for everyday feature work with a clear scope.

claim: Each request includes the current conversation context, so use /clear between unrelated tasks to stop paying for history, even with the 1M-token window most current models have.
why: Old context is discounted while the cache is warm and charged at full price once it expires.
check: Check whether sessions carry unrelated task history into later requests that could start with /clear.
quote: Every request sends the whole conversation, so a session that's collected three unrelated tasks re-reads all three on every turn of the fourth.

claim: The prompt cache lasts about an hour on a subscription and five minutes on an API key, cloud provider, or usage credits, and subagents get five minutes unless changed.
why: Cache expiry turns discounted reads into full-price input.
check: When cache expiry is driving input cost, check how long the main session and subagent requests are idle relative to their cache lifetimes.
quote: lasts about an hour on a subscription and five minutes on an API key, cloud provider, or usage credits.

claim: On Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, and Enterprise, /usage breaks down usage by skill, subagent, plugin, and MCP server and flags patterns such as long context or frequent cache misses above 10% of usage.
why: It is the docs' first stop for finding where tokens go.
check: Use /usage where this breakdown is available to see which extensions or usage patterns account for recurring costs.
quote: It also flags patterns like long context or frequent cache misses once one of them passes 10% of your usage.

claim: The statusline command runs locally and does not consume API tokens, so a context and cost statusline is a free way to watch usage.
why: It reads JSON from stdin (cost.total_cost_usd, context_window.used_percentage) produced client-side.
check: For a local usage display, check whether the status line shows context_window.used_percentage or the estimated cost.total_cost_usd from its input JSON.
quote: The status line runs locally and does not consume API tokens.

claim: The status line estimates cost.total_cost_usd client-side at list price unless modelPricing is in effect, and the estimate resets to $0 when /clear starts a new session.
why: It is an estimate, not billing data.
check: Do not use it as billing truth when judging a change's cost impact.
quote: Estimated session cost in USD, computed client-side at list price unless a [`modelPricing`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#modelpricing) table is in effect. May differ from your actual bill. Resets to \$0 when `/clear` starts a new session

claim: Compaction summaries keep requests and key code but can lose detailed early instructions, so persistent rules belong in CLAUDE.md; a Compact Instructions section or /compact with a focus steers what is kept.
why: Detailed early instructions can be lost when the conversation is summarized.
check: Check whether persistent rules live only in conversation history and look for compaction guidance if specific details need to be retained.
quote: The summary keeps your requests and key code snippets, but detailed instructions from early in the conversation may be lost.

claim: If one file or tool output is so large that context refills right after each summary, Claude Code stops auto-compacting after a few attempts and shows an error rather than looping.
why: It prevents a compaction loop.
check: If a session reports a compaction thrashing error, look for a single file or tool result large enough to refill context immediately after compaction.
quote: Claude Code stops auto-compacting after a few attempts and shows an error instead of looping.

claim: When auto memory is enabled, Claude Code loads the first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md at session start, whichever comes first.
why: The cutoff limits how much of the memory index Claude receives automatically.
check: Check whether auto memory is on and whether entries that need to load at startup fall within both limits.
quote: The first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md, whichever comes first, load at session start while auto memory is on.

claim: Claude Code adds output-style instructions, commit and PR attribution lines, and notices when a file Claude previously edited changes on disk.
why: A system reminder can explain a behavior the user did not specify, such as a Co-Authored-By trailer.
check: For unexpected Git behavior, check attribution for the attribution lines and includeGitInstructions for the built-in commit and pull request instructions.
quote:
A note that a file Claude edited earlier has since changed on disk
* The commit and pull request attribution lines

claim: Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md from the working directory and its parents at startup and loads subdirectory files on demand.
why: Keeping subsystem conventions in per-directory files avoids loading them up front for unrelated work.
check: In a large codebase, check whether subsystem conventions in the root file could move alongside the relevant code.
quote: Claude Code loads every [CLAUDE.md](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory.md) file from your working directory and every parent directory at launch, then loads each subdirectory's file [on demand](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory.md#how-claude-md-files-load). A root file sets repository-wide rules and each subdirectory adds its own.

claim: Within a repository, starting Claude Code in a subdirectory loads its CLAUDE.md and its ancestors' files and gives access to that subtree until you grant more.
why: Starting at the repository root gives access across the repository and loads its subdirectory CLAUDE.md files on demand.
check: Check the starting directory, any extra access grants, and which project settings apply, since settings are not inherited like CLAUDE.md.
quote:
| Repository root | Every file | Root only; subdirectory files load on demand | Tasks span multiple packages or subsystems |
| A subdirectory | That subtree only, until you grant more | That directory's plus every ancestor's | Work is scoped to one package or subsystem |

claim: Use claudeMdExcludes to skip specific CLAUDE.md files for packages you never work in, and start Claude from the relevant package directory when focus changes by task.
why: The exclusion list is static, and matching patterns cannot exclude the organization’s managed CLAUDE.md.
check: Check whether exclusions intended for one person belong in .claude/settings.local.json.
quote: The exclusion list is static, not a per-task switch.

claim: Review CLAUDE.md after major model releases and delete workarounds for old model limitations, since they become overhead once a newer model handles the case.
why: Instructions written for older models can be dead weight.
check: Review old-model workarounds in CLAUDE.md after a major model release and verify whether the newer model still needs each one.
quote: instructions that worked around an older model's limitation may become overhead once a newer model handles the case on its own

claim: Claude's content search respects .gitignore by default, and Read deny rules can block Claude from opening checked-in generated or vendored files.
why: Read deny rules cover built-in file tools and recognized shell reads but cannot stop subprocesses that open files themselves.
check: Check whether irrelevant checked-in paths need a Read deny rule, and distinguish a direct read from a recursive shell search result.
quote:
Claude's content searches respect `.gitignore` by default, so paths already listed there, such as `node_modules/`, `dist/`, and `build/`, stay out of search results.

For paths that are checked in, such as a vendored SDK or committed generated code, add `Read` deny rules in `permissions.deny` to block Claude from opening those files.

claim: The additionalDirectories setting grants file access only, while --add-dir or /add-dir loads skills and can also load CLAUDE.md and rules with CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD=1.
why: Both mechanisms grant read and edit access, but the environment variable has no effect on additionalDirectories entries.
check: If a setup expects a sibling package's conventions to load via additionalDirectories, it will not.
quote:
| `additionalDirectories` setting | Never | Never |
| `--add-dir` flag or `/add-dir` command | Only with the environment variable below | Yes |

claim: Claude uses discovered skill names and available descriptions to select a skill, loads its full content on use, and may drop some descriptions when many skills are in scope.
why: Starting at the repository root can accumulate skills from subdirectories Claude visits.
check: Count skills in scope and check whether their descriptions are short and lead with words likely to appear in requests.
quote: Claude picks a skill by reading every discovered skill's name and description, and only the chosen skill's full content loads into context.

claim: Keep on-demand team procedures in skills and use disable-model-invocation: true for workflows with side effects, so Claude starts those workflows only when you invoke them.
why: For skills Claude can invoke on its own, the name and description load each session and the full content loads when the task calls for it.
check: Look for procedures needed only on some tasks in CLAUDE.md and for side-effect skills Claude can start on its own.
quote: A long release procedure sitting in a skill doesn't weigh on your unrelated bug fix the way it would in `CLAUDE.md`.

claim: For a project skill under .claude/skills/, put SKILL.md in its own directory, since a loose .claude/skills/name.md does not appear in /skills.
why: The debug table lists this as a common cause of missing skills.
check: Check skill file layout.
quote: Use a folder with `SKILL.md` inside: `.claude/skills/name/SKILL.md`.

claim: The commands/*.md directory is the same mechanism as skills, as single-file prompts.
why: The directory reference lists commands/*.md as single-file prompts that use the skill mechanism.
check: When inspecting reusable prompts, include commands/*.md along with skills/<name>/SKILL.md.
quote: Single-file prompts; same mechanism as skills

claim: With feature-flag fetching enabled on Claude Code v2.1.252 or later, /skill-doctor reports skill context cost and usage, and /skills can sort available skills by token count.
why: They are the built-in inspection tools for skill overhead.
check: Use /skill-doctor to find skills with context cost and little usage, or press t in /skills to sort by token count.
quote: Show what each of your [skills](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills.md) costs in context and how often it gets used, so you can [find skills to turn off](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills.md#find-unused-skills). Requires Claude Code v2.1.252 or later

claim: Skill usage can be measured with the OpenTelemetry logs exporter and OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1, which records skill names verbatim; the skill_activated event shows who invoked each skill.
why: It identifies skills to consolidate or retire.
check: If a team asks which skills pay off, point to this telemetry.
quote: set `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1` so skill names are recorded verbatim instead of redacted

claim: Project and user hooks go under the hooks key in settings.json, while plugins can load a separate hooks/hooks.json.
why: Claude Code does not load standalone hook files as project or user configuration.
check: If a hook never fires, verify that it is configured in the project or user settings or loaded as a plugin hook.
quote: There is no standalone hooks file for project or user config. Define hooks under the `"hooks"` key in `settings.json`. Only [plugins](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/components.md#hooks) load a separate `hooks/hooks.json`.

claim: Tool-name hook matchers are case-sensitive strings, use names such as Bash, Edit, Write, and Read, and do not accept JSON arrays.
why: A lowercase tool name can prevent a match, and an array matcher under PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, or PreSkillShellCommand prevents the other hooks in that file from loading.
check: Check for lowercase tool names, array matchers, and comma separators in releases before v2.1.191.
quote: The `matcher` value is an array instead of a single string. Claude Code lists the entry as an invalid setting when you start an interactive session and in `claude doctor`. If the array is under `PreToolUse`, `PermissionRequest`, or `PreSkillShellCommand`, none of that file's other hooks load either.

claim: Project MCP servers go under mcpServers in .mcp.json at the repository root.
why: A project .mcp.json inside .claude/ or an mcpServers key in settings.json will not load those servers.
check: Check .mcp.json location, key name, and whether the one-time project-server approval was dismissed.
quote: Project MCP config goes at the repository root as `.mcp.json`, not inside `.claude/`, with servers under the `mcpServers` key.

claim: ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH defers MCP tools when unset or true where tool search is supported, enables it at 10% of the context window with auto, and loads all tools up front with false.
why: With auto:N you can choose a different percentage threshold for tool definitions.
check: If definitions load up front, check the value of ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH and whether the environment is one where tool search stays off.
quote: Unset or `true` defers MCP tools, except in the [cases that keep tool search off](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md#configure-tool-search). `auto` turns tool search on once definitions reach 10% of the context window. `auto:N` sets a custom threshold, such as `auto:5` for 5%. `false` loads all tools upfront.

claim: Managed settings take precedence, and among other file scopes settings generally resolve local, then project, then user, with some settings also overridable by flags or environment variables.
why: The debug guide names override by another scope or env var as the usual cause.
check: When a setting seems ignored, check the applicable scope, /status for managed sources, and whether the setting has a flag or environment-variable override.
quote: Managed settings apply first when present. Among the rest, the closer scope overrides the broader one in the order local, then project, then user.

claim: The user file ~/.claude.json stores app state and UI toggles, while user permissions, hooks, and env go in ~/.claude/settings.json.
why: Putting config in the wrong file means it is ignored.
check: Check whether user permissions, hooks, or env were placed in ~/.claude.json.
quote: `~/.claude.json` holds app state and UI toggles.

claim: Subdirectory project settings stand on their own, and a session inside a worktree reads the repository root's checked-out .claude/settings.json from the worktree root.
why: Put project hooks and deny rules that the session needs inside worktrees in the repository root's settings file.
check: In monorepos, verify deny rules and hooks exist where worktree and subdirectory sessions will read them.
quote: Project settings inside the worktree therefore load from the worktree root's `.claude/settings.json`, the checked-out copy of the repository root's file.

claim: Project configuration in the directory guide generally lives under .claude/, with CLAUDE.md, .mcp.json, and .worktreeinclude listed at the repository root.
why: The guide lists app state in ~/.claude.json, keybindings, and auto memory as global only.
check: Check the file for each setting or extension, including rules, local settings, skills, commands, output styles, subagents, workflows, and agent memory.
quote: Project-scope files live in your repo under `.claude/` (or at the root for `CLAUDE.md`, `.mcp.json`, and `.worktreeinclude`). Global-scope files live in `~/.claude/` and apply across all projects.

claim: Keep personal project instructions in CLAUDE.local.md and add it to .gitignore, and use .claude/settings.local.json for personal project settings.
why: These files let you keep your own project preferences separate from the team's shared configuration.
check: Check whether personal project instructions and settings that should stay private are kept in ignored local files.
quote: Your personal preferences go in `CLAUDE.local.md` instead of `CLAUDE.md`, and you add that file to `.gitignore` so it stays out of the repo.

claim: Managed settings take precedence over personal settings files and --settings values, subject to narrow exceptions.
why: The settings guide describes exceptions where a more restrictive value can be honored from another scope.
check: Check /status for managed settings sources when auditing organization policy, and verify the effective rules, since the permissions guide says a user-level deny can block a project-level allow.
quote: Enterprise-enforced settings that your own settings files and `--settings` values can't override, apart from [narrow exceptions]

claim: By default, Claude Code stores plaintext session transcripts under ~/.claude/projects, where they can include file contents, command output, pasted text, and loaded instructions.
why: The retention sweep uses cleanupPeriodDays when it can determine it safely, with a default of 30 days and a minimum of 1, while Desktop and Cowork transcripts have separate retention rules.
check: For sessions that may expose credentials, check read-deny rules, transcript retention, and whether CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY is set.
quote: Transcripts and history are not encrypted at rest.

claim: Claude Code keeps file snapshots for the 100 most recent checkpoints in a session, with a checkpoint created for each prompt that starts a turn.
why: Checkpoints are saved with the conversation, and the retention sweep removes snapshots by default about 30 days after the session last saved one.
check: Check whether cleanupPeriodDays retained the snapshots, and use /rewind or /undo, or press Esc twice from NORMAL mode in vim mode or from an empty input outside vim mode.
quote: Claude Code keeps file snapshots for the 100 most recent checkpoints in a session.

claim: Rewind can restore later Bash or subagent edits to files Claude already tracked in the conversation, and it also restores edits from a foreground forked skill.
why: External and other-session edits are normally outside the checkpoint unless they change files tracked in this session, and rewind skips symlinks and hard links.
check: For files changed only by Bash or by an ordinary subagent, check that version control can provide the rollback.
quote: Once Claude has edited a file with its file editing tools in your conversation, `/rewind` undoes changes that Bash commands make to that file afterward. A file that only Bash commands changed isn't tracked and stays as it is.

claim: Resuming appends to the existing session, while /branch or --fork-session forks its history under a new ID.
why: Concurrent resumes of the same session write to one transcript, and a later resume may be missing messages from one run.
check: For concurrent terminals or claude -p runs, check whether each command uses --fork-session when both conversations need to be kept.
quote: If you resume the same session in two terminals or two `claude -p` runs at the same time, both write to one transcript.

claim: Repeat needed launch flags, including --tools, --allowedTools, and --disallowedTools, on ordinary resume, while background sessions keep their flags when reopened live or resumed by full ID with --bg.
why: Ordinary resume also leaves out launch flags for MCP servers, plugins, directories, extra settings, and fallback models.
check: Check that commands using --continue or --resume outside the background-session exceptions repeat the flags for the intended configuration and tool access.
quote: Don't repeat launch flags when you reopen a [background session](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-view.md#what-persists-across-restarts) while it runs, or when you resume it by full session ID with `--bg` after it stops. In both cases, the session keeps its flags.

claim: Claude Code's internal transcript entry format can change between releases, so use /export or the supported script interfaces to build on session data.
why: Non-interactive JSON output and Agent SDK messages provide structured results, while transcript_path identifies the file for uses such as archiving.
check: Check that scripts use a supported interface for structured data and that /export uses a new destination if a filename is supplied on Claude Code v2.1.327 or later.
quote: The entry format is internal to Claude Code and changes between versions, so scripts that parse these files directly can break on any release.

claim: After two failed corrections the docs recommend /clear plus one better prompt instead of a third correction, and Esc or /rewind to steer early.
why: After repeated drift, a fresh prompt lets you start from what you learned instead of adding another correction to the same conversation.
check: When Claude drifts, check whether the user intervenes early and starts fresh after two failed corrections.
quote: after two failed corrections run `/clear` and write a better prompt instead of a third.

claim: Use /context to see what occupies the current window by category, and run /context all in fullscreen mode to expand the per-item breakdown.
why: The breakdown can confirm which memory files, rules, and skill descriptions are present, while nested CLAUDE.md files load on demand when working below the launch directory.
check: Before diagnosing an ignored instruction, inspect /context and verify whether the file should have loaded by that point.
quote: The `/context` command shows everything occupying the context window for the current session.

claim: Use /memory, /skills, /hooks, /mcp, /permissions, and /status to inspect session configuration, with /doctor for a setup checkup and /debug for diagnosis.
why: /debug enables session debug logging and prompts Claude to diagnose the issue using the log output and settings paths.
check: For read-only installation and settings diagnostics without starting a session, run claude doctor.
quote: Enables debug logging for the session and prompts Claude to diagnose using the log output and settings paths

claim: /doctor proposes cuts to CLAUDE.md for information Claude can infer from code, and /doctor prompt-audit flags older-model workarounds, missing file references, and contradictions.
why: They are built-in audits of instruction files.
check: When auditing instruction files, review /doctor's proposed cuts and inspect any issues reported by /doctor prompt-audit.
quote: `/doctor prompt-audit` flags instructions that were written for older models, point at files that no longer exist, or

claim: Use claude --safe-mode to isolate a config problem by disabling customizations such as CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins, and MCP servers while retaining managed hooks and settings policy.
why: Authentication, model selection, built-in tools, and permissions continue to work normally.
check: If the problem persists or settings are suspect, retry from an empty directory with a clean CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR and --setting-sources user.
quote: Safe mode still applies managed hooks and settings policy from your organization. Managed plugins, skills, `CLAUDE.md`, and MCP servers are turned off.

claim: CLAUDE.md adherence drops when instructions are vague, when two files conflict, or when the file is so long that individual rules get less attention; CLAUDE.md is guidance while permissions and hooks enforce limits.
why: When /context confirms the file loaded, the wording or structure of the instruction is a likely cause of poor adherence.
check: After confirming load, review ambiguity, conflicts, and length.
quote: Adherence drops when an instruction is vague enough to interpret multiple ways, when two files give conflicting direction, or when the file has grown long enough that individual rules get less attention.

claim: In scripted runs, --bare skips discovery of repository and machine customizations, and hooks supplied through --settings do not run.
why: You can pass MCP servers explicitly with --mcp-config, and the run uses an API key, an apiKeyHelper in --settings, or cloud credentials instead of your claude.ai login.
check: Check whether the script depends on auto-discovered hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, or CLAUDE.md when it starts in bare mode.
quote: skips your hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, and `CLAUDE.md` files from the repo and your home directory.

claim: An @ reference can include file contents without a tool call, so use a Read deny rule for protected paths or set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FILE_MENTIONS=1 to route reads through file tools.
why: On Claude Code v2.1.299 or later, that variable works in the shell or user or managed settings, while project and local settings ignore it.
check: If PreToolUse hooks control reads, check whether @ includes are blocked for protected paths or switched to file-tool access.
quote: don't run when Claude Code includes a file you reference with `@`, because it makes no tool call.

claim: In Code Mode, the auto-mode classifier normally reviews each piece of JavaScript before it runs, and deny and ask rules and PreToolUse hooks target individual tool calls.
why: The classifier cannot see runtime-computed values, and manual approval of a REPL call can let code start even when the classifier would block it.
check: Check for rules and hooks on individual calls that need control, including whether Bash hooks inspect each part of a compound command.
quote: the classifier reviews each piece of code before it runs, not each tool call.

claim: Set CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW to at least 100000 tokens, and use CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE only to lower the trigger percentage.
why: The environment reference specifies the minimum, and the model configuration guide also documents a 1M cap and clamping to the model context window.
check: Check the configured window against the documented bounds and check that any percentage override lowers the default in a session that compacts before the model limit.
quote: Set the auto-compact window, which is how full the context gets before compaction, to a token count of `100000` or more.

claim: Set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_1M_CONTEXT=1 to hide [1m] model variants and limit models that default to a 1M context window to 200K.
why: The setting turns off Claude Code support for the 1M context window.
check: Check this variable if a model that normally has a 1M window is limited to 200K or a [1m] variant is missing.
quote: Claude Code removes `[1m]` model variants from the model picker and holds models that run with the 1M window by default to a 200K window.

claim: On Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ADAPTIVE_THINKING=1 switches Claude Code to the fixed budget controlled by MAX_THINKING_TOKENS.
why: The switch has no effect on Fable models, Sonnet 5 and later, Haiku 5.5, or Opus 4.7 and later.
check: Check that an intended fixed budget uses a supported model and that adaptive reasoning is disabled for that model.
quote: Set to `1` to disable [adaptive reasoning](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#adjust-effort-level) on Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 and fall back to the fixed thinking budget controlled by `MAX_THINKING_TOKENS`.

claim: For supported models, CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL takes precedence over --effort, /effort, modelSettings, and effortLevel.
why: Available effort levels vary by model, and maxEffortLevel still caps them.
check: Check whether the variable pins a level or is set to auto or unset, which leaves the default to the API.
quote: Takes precedence over `--effort`, `/effort`, and the `modelSettings` and `effortLevel` settings.

claim: On Claude Code v2.1.257 or later, CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1 forces one model onto subagents, teammates, and workflow agents.
why: Without the force setting, CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL is a default that can yield to the invocation or agent definition.
check: If an agent runs on a different model than requested, check whether the force setting overrides the requested model.
quote: Set to `1` to force one model onto subagents, teammates, and workflow agents.

claim: MCP tool output warns above 10,000 tokens and defaults to a 25000-token cap, with a separate character limit for text when the tool declares one.
why: File reads default to 25,000 tokens, and Bash output defaults to 30000 characters with a maximum of 150000 for BASH_MAX_OUTPUT_LENGTH.
check: Check which output limit applies, including whether an MCP tool declares anthropic/maxResultSizeChars for text, a file read uses allow_large, or Bash uses bashOutputMaxChars.
quote: Maximum number of tokens allowed in MCP tool responses (default: 25000).

claim: CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE=1 uses a minimal system prompt and disables automatic discovery of project and user extensions and memory.
why: The baseline tools are Bash, file read, and file edit, with explicit --mcp-config tools still available and --add-dir skills still loaded.
check: For a minimal-configuration baseline, check whether the command explicitly supplies MCP tools or a directory with skills.
quote: Set to `1` to run with a minimal system prompt and the Bash, file read, and file edit tools. MCP tools from `--mcp-config` are still available. OAuth tokens and keychain credentials aren't read, so for the Anthropic API, set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or an `apiKeyHelper` in `--settings`. Equivalent to passing [`--bare`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless#start-faster-with-bare-mode)

claim: Before leaving a run unattended, answer five questions about its completion criteria, verification, allowed scope, stopping cap, and who will receive and approve the result.
why: Unattended runs can keep building on a wrong assumption that a person would catch during an interactive run.
check: Check the definition of done, a runnable check, access limits, a cap such as --max-turns or --max-budget-usd, and where a person receives and approves the result.
quote: Before a run goes unattended, make sure it knows what done looks like, can check its own work, and can only touch what it should.

claim: Use /simplify to review and fix cleanup issues in changed code, and use /code-review to look for correctness bugs.
why: The /simplify reviewers look for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and the right level of abstraction.
check: If the workflow relies on /simplify to find correctness bugs, check whether it should use /code-review for that pass.
quote: The review doesn't look for correctness bugs. Use `/code-review` to find bugs.

claim: /init initializes a project with a CLAUDE.md guide, and CLAUDE_CODE_NEW_INIT=1 enables an interactive flow that also covers skills, hooks, and personal memory files.
why: The interactive flow covers additional configuration alongside the project guide.
check: If the setup expects /init to walk through skills, hooks, and personal memory, check whether CLAUDE_CODE_NEW_INIT is set to 1.
quote: Set `CLAUDE_CODE_NEW_INIT=1` for an interactive flow that also walks through skills, hooks, and personal memory files.

claim: Audit an eval before trusting it, since the most surprising eval results usually turn out to be bugs in the eval rather than facts about the model.
why: A broken eval produces confident numbers pointing the wrong way, and hillclimbing on it multiplies the error.
check: Before accepting a before/after comparison, ask whether the eval itself was audited and run end to end.
quote: In practice the most surprising eval results usually turn out to be bugs in the eval rather than facts about the model

claim: Before the first full eval pass, run a known-good oracle and a null baseline through the whole pipeline, and verify that the oracle passes and the null fails.
why: If the oracle fails the harness or grader is broken, and if the null passes the grader is too lenient.
check: Verify that the oracle passed and the null failed through the full pipeline before the first full eval pass.
quote: If the oracle doesn't pass, the harness or grader is broken; if the null doesn't fail, the grader is too lenient.

claim: Never use one model's outputs as gold when comparing that model with another; reference-match scoring then rewards imitating the incumbent.
why: Reference-match scoring rewards resemblance to the reference model’s output, which can penalize stylistic differences from the incumbent.
check: Check where the expected outputs came from, and consider a rubric, pairwise grading, or human verification of a sample when references are model-generated.
quote: Never use model A's outputs as gold when the question is A vs B.

claim: Keep infrastructure errors separate from eval results, record truncations without averaging them in as wrong, and track refusals as a separate graded outcome.
why: Mixing plumbing failures with genuine model outcomes misattributes failures to the model.
check: Check for a failure-class sidecar for attempts without scorable output, truncation status on clipped rows, and a separate refusal metric.
quote: Rows that did produce output carry `stop_reason` and `status: truncated` when the response hit `max_tokens`, so a clipped answer is counted and shown but not averaged in as wrong. Refusals are a graded outcome, not an error - record them as their own metric so refusal-zeros and capability-zeros aren't summed.

claim: The grader must distinguish a model asserting a negative from a model failing to produce an answer.
why: Otherwise a runner that errors on every input scores like one that carefully found nothing.
check: In detection or classification evals, confirm empty or crashed outputs do not map to the 'none' label.
quote: If both land on the same label, a runner that errors on every input scores identically to one that carefully found nothing.

claim: Run repeated trials and estimate the noise floor at the actual case and rep count: for pass rates, the guide gives roughly 1/sqrt(n·R), or ±14 points at 25 cases and 2 reps.
why: Use the half-width of the paired-difference 95% confidence interval for the baseline target metric.
check: Compare the noise floor with both the remaining headroom and the smallest improvement worth shipping, and flag when the noise floor exceeds either.
quote: for a pass-rate, roughly `1/sqrt(n·R)`: 25 cases × 2 reps ~ ±14 points, 100 × 2 ~ ±7

claim: The eval config must match production: the runner should call the app's real entry point with the same system prompt, tools, model and sampling.
why: A re-implemented call measures a different setup.
check: Diff the eval's actual entry point, system prompt, tools, model version, sampling, and scaffolding against what ships.
quote: The runner must call the app's real entry point; a re-implemented call silently measures a different setup.

claim: For agents that act on an environment, grade the end state (tests pass, diff applies, files present) rather than the transcript, adding a judge only for taste dimensions.
why: A judge reading a coding transcript is grading the narration.
check: Check whether agentic evals inspect the workspace outcome.
quote: A judge reading a coding transcript is grading the narration; the environment is the answer.

claim: Graders should score outcomes, not paths, so a model that solves the task a different valid way is not failed for tool order or phrasing.
why: Path grading penalizes valid solutions.
check: Look for graders that require exact tool-call sequences.
quote: Requiring an exact tool-call sequence, phrasing, or intermediate step fails a model that solved it a different valid way.

claim: When hillclimbing with a train/test split, draw it randomly, stratified by tags[0], without selecting cases by baseline score.
why: Picking only low-scoring training cases steers the analyzer toward the tail and can produce apparent gains from regression to the mean.
check: Check that the split was random and that train and test baseline means agree within noise before the first round.
quote: the split must be drawn at random (stratified by `tags[0]`), never by baseline score.

claim: Disable the tool, memory store, or instruction file the eval is meant to measure and confirm the score drops, then re-enable it and confirm it engages in the transcripts.
why: If the score barely moves either way the eval is not measuring the lever.
check: Check for an ablation run and transcripts showing that the mechanism engages when enabled.
quote: disable it and confirm the score drops; enable it and confirm it engages in the transcripts.

claim: Give an LLM judge a concrete rubric, calibrate it against human labels, and avoid using the exact model under test as its own judge.
why: Position, verbosity, and self-preference can bias scores, so consider a different family or a small jury for close calls.
check: For pairwise grading, randomize order or average both orders, tell the judge to ignore length for its own sake, and revise the judge if agreement on clear cases is well below about 90%.
quote: A judge from the same family as a model under test tends to prefer outputs that resemble its own

claim: Spot-check outputs the grader marked wrong; if more than roughly one in ten look like grader errors, fix the grader before any full pass.
why: Otherwise you are measuring which variant matches the grader's blind spots.
check: Ask whether failures were read by a person.
quote: If more than roughly one in ten look like grader errors, fix the grader before any full pass

claim: Check eval headroom: a baseline near 95% or higher cannot discriminate at the top, and scores near 0% across the board more often indicate a case or grader bug than an impossible task.
why: A near-ceiling hillclimb will mostly move cost or latency, and the last few points can reflect grading or formatting quirks.
check: Compare baseline score and headroom with the effect size sought, and investigate cases and graders when scores are near zero across the board.
quote: If the baseline already scores ~95%+, the eval cannot discriminate at the top

claim: Cover both directions of a behavior (search when needed and not when unneeded), or one-sided evals produce one-sided optimization.
why: An always-search policy would score perfectly on a one-sided eval.
check: For tool-use, refusal or escalation evals, confirm negative cases exist.
quote: otherwise always-search scores perfectly and one-sided evals produce one-sided optimisation

claim: Use API-reported token counts and the actual model's rates, including cache rates, for cost, and time only the final successful request for model latency.
why: String-length estimates can reverse a cost comparison, and including retries can make one variant appear slower.
check: Check for usage-block token counts, actual-model rates, separate judge cost, and a model-latency column that excludes retries, backoff, local queueing, and post-processing.
quote: String-length estimates are off by enough to reverse a cost comparison.

claim: Assert the served model on every call, accepting documented alias-to-snapshot resolution, and save full per-case trajectories so unexpected scores can be traced.
why: A score served by the wrong model measures nothing.
check: Look for response-model assertions and per-case records of messages, tool calls and results, errors, and grader inputs and outputs.
quote: A score served by the wrong model measures nothing

claim: Define specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant success criteria, using several dimensions for most use cases.
why: Vague criteria like 'performs well' cannot be tested.
check: Check that the eval has measurable targets tied to the task and covers each relevant success dimension.
quote: Most use cases need multidimensional evaluation along several success criteria.

claim: The API guide favors more automatically graded questions with slightly lower signal over fewer high-quality, human-graded questions.
why: The recommendation allows a small loss of grading signal in exchange for more questions, while the eval-audit guide separately asks reviewers to verify labels and graders.
check: Check whether automated grading scales coverage while retaining enough signal, and verify label and grader quality before trusting the results.
quote: More questions with slightly lower signal automated grading is better than fewer questions with high-quality human hand-graded evals.

claim: Use code grading where its rules capture the criterion, test LLM judges with clear rubrics before scaling them, and avoid human grading when possible.
why: Code grading is fast and reliable but lacks nuance, while human grading is flexible and high quality but slow and expensive.
check: Check whether each criterion uses the fastest reliable method with enough nuance, and whether LLM grading was tested before scaling.
quote: **Code-based grading:** Fastest and most reliable, extremely scalable, but also lacks nuance for more complex judgments that require less rule-based rigidity.

claim: Design evals to mirror the real task distribution including edge cases such as irrelevant input, overly long input and ambiguous cases.
why: Matching the real task distribution keeps the eval focused on the intended use case, including its edge cases.
check: Compare the case set with real usage and check whether it covers relevant edge cases.
quote: Design evals that mirror your real-world task distribution.

claim: Set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_CLAUDE_MDS=1 to prevent Claude Code from loading CLAUDE.md memory files, including user, project, and auto memory files.
why: The setting keeps those files out of context.
check: If project instructions or auto memory are unexpectedly absent, check whether this variable is set.
quote: Set to `1` to prevent loading any CLAUDE.md memory files into context, including user, project, and auto memory files

claim: MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=0 disables thinking on the Anthropic API where the model allows it, while on third-party providers it omits the thinking parameter.
why: Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, and Fable models do not support turning thinking off.
check: Check the provider and model before treating MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=0 as proof that thinking is disabled.
quote: Set to `0` to disable thinking on the Anthropic API, except on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, and the Fable models, which can't have thinking turned off. On [third-party providers](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/third-party-integrations.md), `0` omits the `thinking` parameter instead.
